title: Edge hedging and circuit harmonization for long-lived LLM streams
creator: Marcus Chen
description:
Background:
Redwood's hosted API edges must maintain strict SLOs for both tail-latency (p99) and availability for long-lived, token-streaming sessions. We periodically see region partial degradations where some edges begin to drop streaming connections or exhibit elevated token latency. Existing failover strategies either do full regional cutovers (causing session loss) or naive hedging which increases duplicate work and costs.

Goal:
Design and implement an active-active 'hedging + circuit harmonization' pattern for our gateway that: (1) preserves active streaming sessions across a regional partial outage where possible, (2) prevents thundering herd and duplicated KV-cache replays, (3) exposes controllable load-shedding and circuit break behavior to meet SLO and cost targets, and (4) provides clear observability and rollback for canary during rollout.

Scope (what this ticket covers):
- Hedge-by-default path for short latency-sensitive requests (eg. non-streaming chat completions) and progressive hedging for long-lived streams.
- Circuit harmonization layer at the gateway to coordinate per-session circuit state across regions without transferring sensitive session payloads.
- Backpressure signaling from compute tier to gateway to drive load-shedding thresholds (latency and CPU pressure).
- Integration points with Console for SLO dashboards and a retriable failure classification in telemetry.
- Automated canary and rollback plan for safe rollout across customer tiers.

Out of scope for this ticket:
- New KV cache replication protocol across regions (we will reuse existing prefix caching and add consistency heuristics).
- Platform cost-billing changes; those will be follow-ups once hedging policy is stable.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Hedging policy implemented in gateway: single-request hedging and progressive N-backup hedging for streams configurable per-route.
2) Circuit harmonizer publishes session circuit state metadata (small non-sensitive tokens) to the routing plane; during partial region failure, gateway can prefer local or remote replicas based on policy and stability.
3) When a region signals degraded status, active-active behavior allows ongoing streams to continue without forced reconnect in >= 80% of simulated partial-outage tests (integration tests in staging).
4) Load-shedding thresholds honor SLOs: when CPU or token-latency exceeds configured thresholds, gateway sheds new ephemeral sessions first, then non-critical backfills, logged with root cause classification.
5) End-to-end latency and token-cost regressions are bounded: p50/p95 within 5% of baseline, p99 reduced to target through hedging/circuit tuning (observability dashboards present comparative curves).
6) Runbook updated and on-call playbook for toggling hedging and circuit harmonizer flags during incidents.
7) Successful canary: < 5% customer impact on tiered canary group; quick rollback path validated through automated playbook.

implementation_notes:
Key decisions: hedging should be adaptive (start off for small latency windows, escalate for repeated token latency spikes). Circuit harmonizer state is intentionally minimal: last-success-timestamp, circuit-token, preferred-region-hint. Hedging must respect per-customer data residency flags and dedicated capacity routing. Backpressure signals carried via existing control plane telemetry; added 'shed-score' per route for progressive eviction.

Trade-offs considered: full KV replication would reduce stream handoffs but is high cost/complexity; we opted for heuristics and warm starts to keep rollout velocity high. Duplicate token work from hedging will be bounded by adaptive cancellation once first response tokens are observed.

Testing plan: unit tests for hedging selector, staged chaos tests simulating partial region CPU exhaustion, long-lived stream resume tests with deterministic token sequences, and a two-week canary starting with internal org and low-volume customers.
